ref: Demonstratio 3 (Robinson's section numbering of the Armenian text)
greek: [Armenian not read; Robinson 1920 English stands in] First of all it bids us bear in mind that we have received baptism for the remission of sins, in the name of God the Father, and in the name of Jesus Christ, the Son of God, who was incarnate and died and rose again, and in the Holy Spirit of God. And that this baptism is the seal of eternal life, and is the new birth unto God, that we should no longer be the sons of mortal men, but of the eternal and perpetual God
greek_edition: Armenian original NOT read. English read from the archive.org OCR text layer (pdftotext) of the SPCK 1920 scan; page image checked for this page.
english: First of all it bids us bear in mind that we have received baptism for the remission of sins, in the name of God the Father, and in the name of Jesus Christ, the Son of God, who was incarnate and died and rose again, and in the Holy Spirit of God. And that this baptism is the seal of eternal life, and is the new birth unto God, that we should no longer be the sons of mortal men, but of the eternal and perpetual God
translator: J. Armitage Robinson (1920), English from the Armenian
edition: London: SPCK, 1920 (Series IV, Oriental Texts; ed. W. K. Lowther Clarke), J. Armitage Robinson, The Demonstration of the Apostolic Preaching
what_it_says: The faith handed down by the Elders is summed up in baptism in the name of God the Father, of Jesus Christ the Son of God, and of the Holy Spirit of God.
limits: Baptismal formula is a confession list, not a doctrine of equality or consubstantiality; no homoousios and no account of eternal generation. The clause 'is made God' in the same section (n. 2: Robinson calls it obscure; Greek theopoieisthai) is not explained here. Robinson's note 3 cites Greek of Haer. I.1.20 (rule of truth), not checked against Harvey.

greek: [Armenian not read; Robinson 1920 English stands in] Thus then there is shown forth One God, the Father, not made, invisible, creator of all things; above whom there is no other God, and after whom there is no other God.
greek_edition: Armenian original NOT read. English read from the archive.org OCR text layer (pdftotext) of the SPCK 1920 scan; page image NOT checked for this page.
english: Thus then there is shown forth One God, the Father, not made, invisible, creator of all things; above whom there is no other God, and after whom there is no other God.
translator: J. Armitage Robinson (1920), English from the Armenian
edition: London: SPCK, 1920 (Series IV, Oriental Texts; ed. W. K. Lowther Clarke), J. Armitage Robinson, The Demonstration of the Apostolic Preaching
what_it_says: The one God is the Father: not made, invisible, creator of all things, with no God above or after him.
limits: The Son and the Spirit are not mentioned in this sentence; Unitarians and polemicists cite 'One God, the Father' and 'no other God' against a divine Son. Robinson's note 1 (on the 'His own' clause just before) notes controversy with heretics who separated the Good God of the Gospels from the Creator. The answer depends on secs. 5-6 (items 03-04).

greek: [Armenian not read; Robinson 1920 English stands in] And, since God is rational, therefore by (the) Word He created the things that were made; and God is Spirit, and by (the) Spirit He adorned all things: as also the prophet says: By the word of the Lord were the heavens established, and by his spirit all their power. Since then the Word establishes, that is to say, gives body and grants the reality of being, and the Spirit gives order and form to the diversity of the powers; rightly and fittingly is the Word called the Son, and the Spirit the Wisdom of God.
greek_edition: Armenian original NOT read. English read from the archive.org OCR text layer (pdftotext) of the SPCK 1920 scan; page image NOT checked for this page.
english: And, since God is rational, therefore by (the) Word He created the things that were made; and God is Spirit, and by (the) Spirit He adorned all things: as also the prophet says: By the word of the Lord were the heavens established, and by his spirit all their power. Since then the Word establishes, that is to say, gives body and grants the reality of being, and the Spirit gives order and form to the diversity of the powers; rightly and fittingly is the Word called the Son, and the Spirit the Wisdom of God.
translator: J. Armitage Robinson (1920), English from the Armenian
edition: London: SPCK, 1920 (Series IV, Oriental Texts; ed. W. K. Lowther Clarke), J. Armitage Robinson, The Demonstration of the Apostolic Preaching
what_it_says: The Word, who is Son, creates and gives being; the Spirit, who is the Wisdom of God, gives order and form.
limits: The Spirit (not the Son) is called Wisdom here. Robinson (intro p. 51 n. 1, item 16) notes that Origen took Wisdom to be the Son, so the Spirit-as-Wisdom identification is a departure Robinson points out. Creation is divided by function, not spelled out as a relation of persons. Robinson's note 2 says 'gives body' is uncertain (Valentinian parallel). Armenian term for 'Wisdom' not checked.

ref: Demonstratio 6 (the three 'points' of the faith; Robinson's section numbering)
greek: [Armenian not read; Robinson 1920 English stands in] God, the Father, not made, not material, invisible; one God, the creator of all things: this is the first point of our faith. The second point is: The Word of God, Son of God, Christ Jesus our Lord, who was manifested to the prophets [...]: through whom all things were made; [...] And the third point is: The Holy Spirit, through whom the prophets prophesied, and the fathers learned the things of God, and the righteous were led forth into the way of righteousness; and who in the end of the times was poured out in a new way upon mankind in all the earth, renewing man unto God.
greek_edition: Armenian original NOT read. English read from the archive.org OCR text layer (pdftotext) of the SPCK 1920 scan; page image checked for this page.
english: God, the Father, not made, not material, invisible; one God, the creator of all things: this is the first point of our faith. The second point is: The Word of God, Son of God, Christ Jesus our Lord, who was manifested to the prophets [...]: through whom all things were made; [...] And the third point is: The Holy Spirit, through whom the prophets prophesied, and the fathers learned the things of God, and the righteous were led forth into the way of righteousness; and who in the end of the times was poured out in a new way upon mankind in all the earth, renewing man unto God.
translator: J. Armitage Robinson (1920), English from the Armenian
edition: London: SPCK, 1920 (Series IV, Oriental Texts; ed. W. K. Lowther Clarke), J. Armitage Robinson, The Demonstration of the Apostolic Preaching
what_it_says: The rule of faith has three points: God the Father; the Word, Son of God, Christ Jesus our Lord, through whom all things were made; and the Holy Spirit.
limits: The text says 'three points', not 'three articles' (phrase searched, not found). Ellipses mark omitted clauses (the manifestation and dispensation clause; the Incarnation clause). The Son and the Spirit are not called 'God' in this passage ('Word of God', 'Son of God'). No 'persons' or homoousios language. Robinson's notes give Book IV parallels (not checked).

greek: [Armenian not read; Robinson 1920 English stands in] And for this reason the baptism of our regeneration proceeds through these three points: God the Father bestowing on us regeneration through His Son by the Holy Spirit. [...] Without the Spirit it is not possible to behold the Word of God, nor without the Son can any draw near to the Father: for the knowledge of the Father is the Son, and the knowledge of the Son of God is through the Holy Spirit; and, according to the good pleasure of the Father, the Son ministers and dispenses the Spirit to whomsoever the Father wills and as He wills.
greek_edition: Armenian original NOT read. English read from the archive.org OCR text layer (pdftotext) of the SPCK 1920 scan; page image NOT checked for this page.
english: And for this reason the baptism of our regeneration proceeds through these three points: God the Father bestowing on us regeneration through His Son by the Holy Spirit. [...] Without the Spirit it is not possible to behold the Word of God, nor without the Son can any draw near to the Father: for the knowledge of the Father is the Son, and the knowledge of the Son of God is through the Holy Spirit; and, according to the good pleasure of the Father, the Son ministers and dispenses the Spirit to whomsoever the Father wills and as He wills.
translator: J. Armitage Robinson (1920), English from the Armenian
edition: London: SPCK, 1920 (Series IV, Oriental Texts; ed. W. K. Lowther Clarke), J. Armitage Robinson, The Demonstration of the Apostolic Preaching
what_it_says: The Son ministers and dispenses the Spirit according to the Father's good pleasure, to whom and as the Father wills.
limits: Objection: the Son acts on the Father's will and gives the Spirit (subordinationist reading). Robinson's note 4 says the verb is uncertain and renders it 'ministerially dispenses'; it cross-refers to V.18.1 (Latin 'Verbum praestat Spiritum omnibus quemadmodum vult Pater'), not checked. 'The knowledge of the Father is the Son' is Robinson's n. 3 citing IV.11.5 (Latin, not checked). Ellipsis marks omitted 'For as many as carry the Spirit' clause.

greek: [Armenian not read; Robinson 1920 English stands in] Now this God is glorified by His Word who is His Son continually, and by the Holy Spirit who is the Wisdom of the Father of all: and the power(s) of these, (namely) of the Word and Wisdom, which are called Cherubim and Seraphim, with unceasing voices glorify God; and every created thing that is in the heavens offers glory to God the Father of all.
greek_edition: Armenian original NOT read. English read from the archive.org OCR text layer (pdftotext) of the SPCK 1920 scan; page image checked for this page.
english: Now this God is glorified by His Word who is His Son continually, and by the Holy Spirit who is the Wisdom of the Father of all: and the power(s) of these, (namely) of the Word and Wisdom, which are called Cherubim and Seraphim, with unceasing voices glorify God; and every created thing that is in the heavens offers glory to God the Father of all.
translator: J. Armitage Robinson (1920), English from the Armenian
edition: London: SPCK, 1920 (Series IV, Oriental Texts; ed. W. K. Lowther Clarke), J. Armitage Robinson, The Demonstration of the Apostolic Preaching
what_it_says: God is glorified by his Word, who is his Son, and by the Holy Spirit, who is the Wisdom of the Father of all.
limits: The brief's wording 'the Father, the Son, the Spirit' is not in this section; the text is 'glorified by His Word ... and by the Holy Spirit'. 'Continually' is uncertain (Robinson's n. 4: German translators read 'eternal'). The Cherubim/Seraphim framing is liturgical and does not state equality. Robinson cross-refers to intro p. 39 (liturgical parallel, Serapion).

greek: [Armenian not read; Robinson 1920 English stands in] But man He formed with His own hands, taking from the earth that which was purest and finest, and mingling in measure His own power with the earth. For He traced His own form on the formation, that that which should be seen should be of divine form: for (as) the image of God was man formed and set on the earth,

For He traced His own form on the formation, that that which should be seen should be of divine form: for (as) the image of God was man formed and set on the earth,
translator: J. Armitage Robinson (1920), English from the Armenian
edition: London: SPCK, 1920 (Series IV, Oriental Texts; ed. W. K. Lowther Clarke), J. Armitage Robinson, The Demonstration of the Apostolic Preaching
what_it_says: God formed man with his own hands, and man bears the divine image.
limits: Section 11 says only 'His own hands'. That the hands are the Son and the Spirit is Robinson's n. 1 (citing intro p. 51, item 16), not this passage. Robinson notes the Latin 'figuratio sua' problem (intro p. 51 n. 3). Read alone, the hands could be the Father's own power, which critics will press.

greek: [Armenian not read; Robinson 1920 English stands in] that after the flesh He might be the son of David, who was the son of Abraham by a long succession; but according to the spirit Son of God, pre-existing with the Father, begotten before all the creation of the world, and at the end of the times appearing to all the world as man, the Word of God gathering up in Himself all things that are in heaven and that are on earth.
greek_edition: Armenian original NOT read. English read from the archive.org OCR text layer (pdftotext) of the SPCK 1920 scan; page image checked for this page.
english: that after the flesh He might be the son of David, who was the son of Abraham by a long succession; but according to the spirit Son of God, pre-existing with the Father, begotten before all the creation of the world, and at the end of the times appearing to all the world as man, the Word of God gathering up in Himself all things that are in heaven and that are on earth.
translator: J. Armitage Robinson (1920), English from the Armenian
edition: London: SPCK, 1920 (Series IV, Oriental Texts; ed. W. K. Lowther Clarke), J. Armitage Robinson, The Demonstration of the Apostolic Preaching
what_it_says: The Son of God, according to the spirit, pre-exists with the Father, is begotten before creation, and appears as man in the last times.
limits: 'Begotten before all the creation' is temporal-priority language that Arian and other critics read as a created Son ('there was when he was not'); the text does not say 'eternal' or 'consubstantial'. Robinson's n. 2 cross-refers to sec. 51 for 'pre-existing'.

greek: [Armenian not read; Robinson 1920 English stands in] Now that there was a Son of God, and that He existed not only before He appeared in the world, but also before the world was made, Moses, who was the first that prophesied, says in Hebrew: [Hebrew transliteration of Gen. 1.1 omitted]. And this, translated into our language, is: 'The Son in the beginning: God established then the heaven and the earth.' This Jeremiah the prophet also testified, saying thus: Before the morning-star I begat thee: and before the sun [...] thy name; and that is, before the creation of the world; [...] Because, for God, the Son was (as) the beginning before the creation of the world;
greek_edition: Armenian original NOT read. English read from the archive.org OCR text layer (pdftotext) of the SPCK 1920 scan; page image NOT checked for this page.
english: Now that there was a Son of God, and that He existed not only before He appeared in the world, but also before the world was made, Moses, who was the first that prophesied, says in Hebrew: [Hebrew transliteration of Gen. 1.1 omitted]. And this, translated into our language, is: 'The Son in the beginning: God established then the heaven and the earth.' This Jeremiah the prophet also testified, saying thus: Before the morning-star I begat thee: and before the sun [...] thy name; and that is, before the creation of the world; [...] Because, for God, the Son was (as) the beginning before the creation of the world;
translator: J. Armitage Robinson (1920), English from the Armenian
edition: London: SPCK, 1920 (Series IV, Oriental Texts; ed. W. K. Lowther Clarke), J. Armitage Robinson, The Demonstration of the Apostolic Preaching
what_it_says: The Son existed before the world; Irenaeus reads Gen. 1.1 as 'In the beginning the Son' and the Jeremiah texts as showing pre-creation existence.
limits: Critics cite 'the Son was (as) the beginning' with Prov. 8:22 (Robinson's n. 6: 'probably a reference' to LXX Prov. 8:22). Robinson n. 3: the Hebrew is corrupted and Irenaeus reads 'In the beginning' as 'the Son'. Irenaeus attributes 'before the morning-star I begat thee' to Jeremiah; Robinson (n. 4) says it is a composite of Psalms (intro pp. 10ff.), and 'Blessed is he who was, before he became man' is in no known book of Jeremiah (intro p. 22). Ellipses mark the omitted Hebrew transliteration, Robinson's marginal reference (Ps. lxxii. 17), and the omitted 'Blessed is he who was' and 'the stars were made' clauses. Sec. 43 begins 'So then we must believe God in all things' (not quoted).

greek: [Armenian not read; Robinson 1920 English stands in] So then the Father is Lord and the Son is Lord, and the Father is God and the Son is God; for that which is begotten of God is God. And so in the substance and power of His being there is shown forth one God; but there is also according to the economy of our redemption both Son and Father. Because to created things the Father of all is invisible and unapproachable, therefore those who are to draw near to God must have their access to the Father through the Son.
greek_edition: Armenian original NOT read. English read from the archive.org OCR text layer (pdftotext) of the SPCK 1920 scan; page image NOT checked for this page.
english: So then the Father is Lord and the Son is Lord, and the Father is God and the Son is God; for that which is begotten of God is God. And so in the substance and power of His being there is shown forth one God; but there is also according to the economy of our redemption both Son and Father. Because to created things the Father of all is invisible and unapproachable, therefore those who are to draw near to God must have their access to the Father through the Son.
translator: J. Armitage Robinson (1920), English from the Armenian
edition: London: SPCK, 1920 (Series IV, Oriental Texts; ed. W. K. Lowther Clarke), J. Armitage Robinson, The Demonstration of the Apostolic Preaching
what_it_says: The Father is Lord and God, the Son is Lord and God, because what is begotten of God is God; one God is shown in the substance and power of his being.
limits: Strongest sentence in this work for the Son's deity, but 'substance' is Robinson's rendering of an uncertain Armenian term, and 'economy of our redemption' distinguishes the Father and Son in the economy. Robinson's n. 2 quotes Greek 'to gar ek theou gennēthen theos estin' with a reference that OCR garbles ('7, 1. 18'); not checked. Next section (48) has 'receives from the Father' language (item 11).

greek: [Armenian not read; Robinson 1920 English stands in] Now hereby he proclaimed that He came into being before all, and that He rules over the Gentiles and judges all mankind and the kings who now hate Him and persecute His name; for these are His enemies: and in calling Him God's priest for ever, he declared His immortality. And therefore he said: He shall drink of the brook in the way; therefore shall he lift up the head; proclaiming the exaltation with glory that followed on His humanity and humiliation and ingloriousness.

And therefore he said: He shall drink of the brook in the way; therefore shall he lift up the head; proclaiming the exaltation with glory that followed on His humanity and humiliation and ingloriousness.
translator: J. Armitage Robinson (1920), English from the Armenian
edition: London: SPCK, 1920 (Series IV, Oriental Texts; ed. W. K. Lowther Clarke), J. Armitage Robinson, The Demonstration of the Apostolic Preaching
what_it_says: Psalm 110 is read of the Son: he 'came into being before all', is priest for ever, and was exalted after his humanity and humiliation.
limits: 'Came into being' is the Armenian rendering in Robinson's English; the Greek verb is not read, so an Arian reading of 'created' cannot be checked here. The exaltation 'that followed on His humanity and humiliation' is the economy answer. Robinson's n. 3 cites Justin Dial. 33 for 'humiliation first, then exaltation'.

[...] For he means that the Father speaks with the Son; [...] Forasmuch as David says: The Lord said unto me, it is necessary to say that it is not David who speaks, nor any one of the prophets, in his own person: for it is not a man who speaks the prophecies; but the Spirit of God, assimilating and likening Himself to the persons represented, speaks in the prophets, and utters the words sometimes from Christ and sometimes from the Father.

[...] For he means that the Father speaks with the Son; [...] Forasmuch as David says: The Lord said unto me, it is necessary to say that it is not David who speaks, nor any one of the prophets, in his own person: for it is not a man who speaks the prophecies; but the Spirit of God, assimilating and likening Himself to the persons represented, speaks in the prophets, and utters the words sometimes from Christ and sometimes from the Father.

Ellipses mark omitted Isaiah and psalm clauses.

greek: [Armenian not read; Robinson 1920 English stands in] Here, first of all, is seen that the Son of God pre-existed, from the fact that the Father spake with Him, and before He was born revealed Him to men: and, next, that He must needs be born a man among men; [...] And that the Son of the Father calls Himself servant, (this is) on account of His subjection to the Father: for among men also every son is the servant of his father.

translator: J. Armitage Robinson (1920), English from the Armenian
edition: London: SPCK, 1920 (Series IV, Oriental Texts; ed. W. K. Lowther Clarke), J. Armitage Robinson, The Demonstration of the Apostolic Preaching
what_it_says: The Son pre-existed, since the Father spoke with him; he calls himself servant because of his subjection to the Father, as a son is a servant of his father among men.
limits: Answers the servant objection but concedes 'subjection' as the economy; the son/father analogy gives the Father priority. Robinson's n. 2 cross-refers to sec. 30 and Justin Dial. 62 ('the offspring ... was with the Father before all creatures'). Ellipsis marks omitted clauses on the Son's birth of the Spirit and of the Jews.

greek: [Armenian not read; Robinson 1920 English stands in] That Christ, then, being Son of God before all the world, is with the Father; and being with the Father is also nigh and close and joined unto mankind; and is King of all, because the Father has subjected all things unto Him; and Saviour of them that believe on Him—such things do the Scriptures declare.
greek_edition: Armenian original NOT read. English read from the archive.org OCR text layer (pdftotext) of the SPCK 1920 scan; page image NOT checked for this page.

translator: J. Armitage Robinson (1920), English from the Armenian
edition: London: SPCK, 1920 (Series IV, Oriental Texts; ed. W. K. Lowther Clarke), J. Armitage Robinson, The Demonstration of the Apostolic Preaching

ref: Robinson 1920 Introduction, pp. 50-51 (on Demonstratio 10-11 and Adv. haer. IV pref. 3)
greek: [Armenian not read; Robinson 1920 English stands in] This equivalence in creative function of the Son and the Spirit, as the Word and the Wisdom of God, is strangely expressed in Bks. IV and V, by calling them the Hands of God. In IV, pref. 3 we read: 'Man is a mingling of soul and flesh, fashioned after the likeness of God and formed [...] by His Hands, that is, by the Son and the Spirit, to whom also He said: Let us make man.'
greek_edition: Robinson 1920 introduction (English only). Page image not checked; OCR text layer.
english: This equivalence in creative function of the Son and the Spirit, as the Word and the Wisdom of God, is strangely expressed in Bks. IV and V, by calling them the Hands of God. In IV, pref. 3 we read: 'Man is a mingling of soul and flesh, fashioned after the likeness of God and formed [...] by His Hands, that is, by the Son and the Spirit, to whom also He said: Let us make man.'
edition: London: SPCK, 1920 (Series IV, Oriental Texts; ed. W. K. Lowther Clarke), J. Armitage Robinson, The Demonstration of the Apostolic Preaching
what_it_says: Robinson reads the Son and the Spirit, as Word and Wisdom, as the Hands of God in Books IV and V.
limits: Robinson's commentary, not Irenaeus. The English of Adv. haer. IV pref. 3 is Robinson's translation of the Latin, not checked. Robinson n. 1: Origen found the Spirit in Gen. 1.2 but held Wisdom to be the Son. Ellipsis marks the word OCR read as 'f/asmatus' (plasmatus, not confirmed). Introduction page image not checked.
